content: 1. A legally authorized representative must provide consent in accordance with applicable laws when the individual is unable to do so. Waiving informed consent is considered rare and exceptional, and it must always be approved by an ethical review committee. 2. Before obtaining an individual’s consent to participate in research, the investigator must provide clear and understandable information, including: The invitation to participate in research, the reasons for considering the individual suitable, and the voluntary nature of participation. The individual’s right to refuse participation or withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of entitled benefits. The purpose of the research, the procedures involved, and how the research differs from routine medical care. Any study design elements, such as randomization or blinding, and the fact that the assigned treatment will not be disclosed until the study concludes. The expected duration of participation, including the number and length of visits, and the possibility of early termination of the trial or the individual’s participation. Whether monetary or material compensation will be provided, and the type and amount of such compensation. That participants will be informed of the general findings of the research and any findings relevant to their health status after the study concludes. The right of participants to access their data upon request, even if the data lacks immediate clinical utility, unless non-disclosure has been approved by the ethical review committee. Any foreseeable risks, pain, discomfort, or inconvenience associated with participation, including risks to the participant’s spouse or partner. The direct benefits, if any, expected from participation. The expected benefits of the research to the community or society, or its contribution to scientific knowledge. Whether proven safe and effective interventions or products will be made available to participants after the study, and whether participants will need to pay for them. Any currently available alternative interventions or treatments. Provisions to ensure respect for participants’ privacy and confidentiality of their records. The limits to the investigators’ ability to safeguard confidentiality and the potential consequences of breaches. The sponsors of the research, the investigators’ institutional affiliations, and the sources of funding. The possible research uses of participants’ medical records and biological specimens, including whether specimens will be destroyed or stored for future use, and participants’ rights to refuse storage or request destruction. Whether commercial products may be developed from biological specimens and whether participants will receive any benefits from such developments. Whether the investigator is acting solely as a researcher or also as the participant’s physician. The extent of the investigator’s responsibility to provide medical care to participants. That free treatment will be provided for research-related injuries or complications, including the nature, duration, and funding of such care. How participants or their families will be compensated for disability or death resulting from research-related injuries, or if no compensation plans exist. Whether the right to compensation is legally guaranteed in the country where the research is conducted. That the research protocol has been approved by an ethical review committee. 3. Sponsors and investigators must avoid unjustified deception, undue influence, or intimidation when seeking informed consent. They must ensure that prospective participants fully understand the relevant facts and consequences of participation and have sufficient time to decide. 4. Investigators must generally obtain a signed informed consent form from each participant, with exceptions requiring justification and ethical review committee approval. In long-term studies, informed consent must be renewed at predetermined intervals or when significant changes occur in the research. 5. Participants may be reimbursed for lost earnings, travel costs, and other expenses incurred during the study. They may also receive free medical services. Payments or compensation must not be so large as to unduly influence participants to consent against their better judgment. All payments and services must be approved by an ethical review committee. 6. Investigators must ensure that the potential benefits and risks of research are reasonably balanced and that risks are minimized. Interventions offering direct diagnostic, therapeutic, or preventive benefits must be justified by their expected advantages compared to available alternatives. Risks of interventions without direct benefits must be justified by their societal value and the importance of the knowledge to be gained. 7. When research involves individuals incapable of giving informed consent, the risks of non-beneficial interventions must not exceed those of routine medical or psychological examinations. Slight increases in risk may be permitted if justified by overriding scientific or medical rationale and approved by an ethical review committee. 8. Research in resource-limited populations or communities must address their health needs and priorities. Any interventions, products, or knowledge generated must be made reasonably available to benefit the population or community. 9. In clinical trials, control group participants should generally receive an established effective intervention. Placebos may be used only when no effective intervention exists, when withholding treatment poses minimal risk, or when scientifically reliable results cannot be obtained otherwise. 10. Research groups or communities must be selected to ensure equitable distribution of burdens and benefits. Exclusion of groups that might benefit from participation must be justified. 11. Special justification is required for involving vulnerable individuals in research. Their rights and welfare must be strictly protected. 12. Research involving children must ensure that it cannot be equally well conducted with adults, that it addresses children’s health needs, and that parental permission and the child’s assent are obtained. A child’s refusal to participate must be respected. 13. Research involving individuals with mental or behavioral disorders must ensure that such individuals are not included if the research can be conducted with those capable of informed consent. The research must address their specific health needs, and their consent must be obtained to the extent of their capabilities. Refusal to participate must be respected unless exceptional circumstances apply. 14. Women of reproductive age should not be excluded from research solely due to the potential for pregnancy. Risks to pregnant women and their fetuses must be thoroughly discussed, and effective contraception and pregnancy testing should be provided when necessary. 15. Pregnant women should be presumed eligible for research participation if the research addresses their health needs or those of their fetuses. Risks and benefits must be clearly communicated, and research should be supported by reliable evidence, particularly regarding teratogenicity and mutagenicity. 16. Investigators must establish secure safeguards to protect the confidentiality of participants’ research data. Participants must be informed of the limits to confidentiality and the potential consequences of breaches. 17. Research participants who suffer injuries as a result of their participation are entitled to free medical treatment and equitable compensation for any resulting impairment or disability.
